It is hardly necessary to say that I would be as reluctant as anyone to send a coloured person back to South Africa. However, that is not the immediate issue. Suggestions have been made that Mr. Peterson should have been acceptable in the ordinary way and was refused because of racial bias. I should say that the reporter who purported to make an assessment of his qualifications did not take the trouble to study the regulations carefully. For example, he wanted to give Mr. Peterson ten points for languages, whereas the maximum available for fluency in one of our

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, October 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner for the second reading of Bill No. C-161, to establish a department of corporate and consumer affairs.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate on the bill to establish a department of corporate and consumer affairs was adjourned yesterday afternoon I was in the process of pointing out that the most glaring omission in this legislation is the failure of the government to make any provision for coping with the problem of the rising cost of living. I was pointing out that the cost of living has been rising rapidly and that this rise has been accelerated in recent months.
Since the present government took office in the spring of 1963 the cost of living has gone up by some 18 percentage points, or an increase of 13.5 per cent. This means that the purchasing power of the dollar in a store today is 86J cents compared with what it was when this government took office. The most serious aspect of this situation, however, is that the rise in the cost of living has been accelerated in recent months. In the first nine months of this calendar year the cost of living has gone up by 4.7 per cent, and it is a fairly safe prediction that for the entire year 1967 the cost of living will go up by some 5 per cent.
3266	COMMONS
Corporate and Consumer Affairs
This is the problem that is concerning the housewives of Canada and the people of this country generally. I noticed in yesterday's Montreal Star that a Gallup poll had been held with regard to the new department of corporate and consumer affairs. Of those people interviewed who were familiar with the fact that such a department was being set up, the great majority considered that the most important problem which ought to be dealt with by the government was the control of profits and prices. It is interesting that the Gallup poll shows that only some 5 per cent were concerned about proper weights and clearer labels on packaging, some 4 per cent were concerned with the control of advertising and the need to stop misleading advertising, only 1 per cent were concerned about give-aways and fraud, but 45 per cent felt that the most important question with which the government had to grapple was the controlling of prices and profits.
This is precisely what the government is refusing to do in this legislation. It is true that the minister has shown his tearful sympathy for the poor consumer. As reported at page 3213 of Hansard, he expressed that sympathy in eloquent terms when he said:
I think in particular of the low income consumer who must use his dollar with effectiveness. He must gain fair access to quality goods at low prices and be protected against unfair selling and credit practices. There is the elderly consumer who has special health, housing and nutritional needs- needs shown by those with disabilities. Then there is the rural consumer who has difficulty in gaining full access to the urban market because of the distance he or she is from that market.
Those are very genuine concerns which the minister has expressed. Let me go on to show, however, the solution which he offers. He went on to say:
It will be our concern to search out and explore the ways of servicing these particular problems-
That is not much consolation. The minister could very well put on a soap opera in which, with tears in his eyes, he could deplore the state of the elderly, the housewives and the disabled and then finish by singing "I Can't Give You Anything But Love, Baby."

speechtext:
The minister prides himself on being very modern and up to date. That, of course, is what one would expect from a young man on the make. He delivered himself of a little homily the other evening, as

recorded at page 3206 of Hansard, when he said:
Each new morning brings some obsolescence to some aspect of our lives. Unless we are prepared to re-examine on a daily basis, to reassess and revalue what we do and how we do it, we are in danger of falling behind and becoming irrelevant to contemporary needs. Nowhere is this more true than in dealing with our economy.
I agree with the minister 100 per cent. No one could disagree with such a general statement about the need for removing obsolescence, for changing with changing conditions. But when the minister comes to grapple with the real problems which are facing the consumer, what do we find him saying? We find him saying, as reported at page 3210 of Hansard:
-there is no intention that this department should act as a sort of controller-
On the same page he said:
-I tend to be convinced that attempts in peacetime to regulate prices by law would shortly prove to be unworkable and inconsistent with the operation of a market economy.
When the minister talks like that he is revealing himself as a Rip Van Winkle.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext: Who is not yet awake.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
Surely the minister ought to know that the day when the market could be considered as the arbiter of man's economic destiny is long past, if it ever did exist. Surely the myth that the free play of the market will protect the producer and the consumer is as dead as the dodo. In his recent book "The New Industrial State" J. K. Galbraith points out quite convincingly that we no longer live in a day when the free play of the market provides any protection whatsoever. The only people who still believe that the marketplace is allowed to operate freely are those who are mentally living in the era of nineteenth century Liberalism.
As Mr. Galbraith points out, in the United States alone some 500 corporations produce over 50 per cent of all the goods and services of that country. He said that these corporations, because of the fact that they require very large sums of capital, because they require highly skilled and specialized labour forces, and because they must do long-term planning both with respect to their supplies and to the demand for their products, have now reached the point where they manipulate the market and control the supply and demand. They exercise influence upon buying patterns so we no longer have a free market, and the market cannot possibly provide any protection for the consumer.
October 19, 1967	COMMONS
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
For any person today to talk about intervention by the government with respect to prices as being inconsistent with a market economy is to reveal that that person has ideas that are as out of date as Methuselah. I say to the minister that he must modernize his thinking. We live in a technological society in which giant corporations control the market, set prices and manipulate supply and demand, and the consumer is left defenceless and helpless in that situation.
We cannot resolve this problem by turning back the clock of history. Big corporations cannot be reduced to small corporations. Bigness itself is not a vice. Big corporations are an essential concomitant of a technological society. This is particularly true in regard to the mass production of steel, automobiles and most of the extraction industries. Our economy now requires large corporations with a large amount of capital, long-term planning, research facilities and highly specialized technical skills. It is not possible to go back to the nineteenth century with innumerable small corporations. The giant corporations are here and the economic concentration of power is in their hands. There is no way that this trend can be reversed. But what the government can and must do in that situation is intervene to protect the consumer and unless the government is prepared to do so then, of course, the consumers will be exploited as they have been over the years.
Who else is going to protect the consumer in this country unless the government does so? Who else is going to do something about the fact that we are manufacturing cars in this country under the Canada-United States auto trade agreement and the companies are selling Canadian made cars in the United States for less than they are sold in Canada? Who else is going to protect the farming population whose average price index has been more or less stationary ever since 1951, while in the last three years alone the cost of the things they must buy in order to produce has gone up by 17 per cent? Who else is going to protect the farmer from the rapid increase in the cost of farm machinery so that Massey-Ferguson, for instance, could increase its profits between 1964 and 1966 from $18,100,000 to $45,200,000, an increase of 150 per cent, although its sales increased in that period only by some 56 per cent? Who is going to protect the consumer against unconscionable profiteering by the pharmaceutical companies and the exorbitant prices which they charge for drugs which are absolutely 27053-2071

Who else is going to protect the housewife who has to buy in the great chain stores where prices are maintained by what has now become a virtual monopoly of the food industries? Who else is going to protect the public against fixed retail prices, particularly for electrical appliances?
All along the line the consumer finds himself in a marketplace dominated by gigantic corporations, and the government has the responsibility to protect the consumer. That is what the consumers asked for when they were urging this parliament to do something two years ago. It was to meet this problem that a committee on consumer credit and prices was set up.
All we now have is a piece of legislation which deals with the peripheral problems and fails entirely to deal with the problem of the rising cost of living. There is nothing in this legislation which will protect the housewife, the person buying drugs, the farmer paying exorbitant prices for farm machinery, the consumer paying a very high price for automobiles compared with the price of automobiles in the United States.
I invite the minister, before he closes this debate, to tell the house where in this legislation the Canadian consumer has any protection at all with respect to inordinate and unconscionable profiteering on the part of these large corporations. The minister of course takes refuge in the constitution. He says that the federal government does not have the constitutional power to enter this field. I have been listening to the Liberals excusing their inactivity for a quarter of a century by finding refuge in the constitution. We were told for years that we could not have a wheat board to handle the farmers' wheat and their coarse grains because there were constitutional difficulties. But we found a way through those constitutional difficulties and we now have a wheat board. We were told for years we could not have universal old age pensions and we could not have family allowances because there were constitutional difficulties. The fact is that we found ways of amending the constitution so as to overcome those difficulties. I listened for years to successive governments saying we could not have medicare in Canada because there were constitutional difficulties, but when governments really want to carry out a program they can find the constitutional solution to those difficulties.
October 19, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs
I think the government has to begin byremembering that the constitution was made for man, not man for the constitution, that there is nothing sacrosanct about a constitution. It is not the law of the Medes and the Persians. The constitution is the framework within which we operate and, as the minister himself has said, we live within a society where the basic law is the law of change, and with technological change there must not only be social and economic changes but there must also be constitutional changes. The constitution really does not offer any insurmountable obstacle to grappling with the problem of the rising cost of living, e (3:40 p.m.)
The minister, in speaking of my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis), said she was apparently trying to bring about a reincarnation of the wartime prices control board. That is an indication of antediluvian thinking. Nobody is suggesting to the minister that he should set up a wartime prices control board. We in this party have suggested two things to the minister which he should do and which he can do within the constitutional framework of this country. The first thing we have suggested is that there should be set up within the department of corporate and consumer affairs a prices review board. The function of that board would be to investigate to what extent increases in prices of basic commodities are justified. We readily admit that if an industry finds its costs have risen, its labour costs per unit of production, its fuel costs, its raw material costs, its transportation costs, then that company must have an increase in price. No company can stay in business and show a loss year after year.
But what we are saying is that industry should have to justify its price increases. The laws of this country require that when a trade union is in the process of bargaining collectively it must go before a conciliation board and seek to justify its demands for increases in rates. Is there any reason why the basic industries of this country which increase prices to the consumer should not be required to justify the price increases that they are going to levy upon the Canadian public?
Let us take the steel industry as an example. The last time they raised the price of steel it was shown that the labour cost per ton of steel had actually declined by $5.36 per ton. The steel industry, during a five year period, had increased its profits by some 106 per cent. Hon. members know that

increases in the price of steel affect the whole economy. They automatically mean increases in the prices of cars, tractors, trucks, farm implements and even houses. There is hardly a commodity that either does not contain steel or is not made by machines which contain steel. Consequently, an increase in the price of steel has an inflationary effect on the whole economy.
The International Nickel Company, which has a virtual monopoly on the production and sale of nickel, increased its prices despite the fact its profits are higher than at any time in its history. Farm implement companies raised their prices at a time when their profits had reached record heights. Surely the Canadian people are entitled to some protection. Surely the government has the constitutional power to at least require an investigation to ascertain whether or not these companies are justified in raising their prices or whether the increases in prices simply represent taking advantage of the fact they are in a seller's market.
The Canadian people have the right to know whether price increases are the result of certain economic factors such as increased costs or whether those increases are the result of greedy, exorbitant profiteering. This is what we ask the government to do. We ask them to set up a prices review board. We have been making this request for the last four years, but the government has failed to act. There is no constitutional obstacle which stands in the way of setting up such a prices review board. This information would then be available to the Canadian people. The Canadian people would then know whether or not price increases were justified or unwarranted.
The second thing the government could do, if they found certain industries were taking advantage of the public, were fleecing the consumer, would be to ask the provinces for concurrent legislation to compel that particular industry to put its price back to the former level. We are not suggesting for a moment that we should have a wartime prices control board. The situation which exists now is not similar to wartime when there were shortages of certain materials which were essential for defence production. What we are saying is that there may have to be selective controls in respect of certain basic commodities if it is revealed by the prices review board that there have been unwarranted price increases.
I cannot see any provincial legislature in Canada refusing to give assent to concurrent
October 19, 19S7	COMMONS
legislation requiring an industry to reduce its price to a former level if the prices review board revealed beyond any doubt that the price increases were unjustified.

PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I should say a few words on Bill C-161, an "Act to establish a department of corporate and consumer affairs." In my opinion, this department may become the biggest and the most important one we have, since it will be responsible for informing and protecting the consumer, for it must not be forgotten that although we have about seven million Canadians who work, seven million Canadian producers, there are more than twenty million consumers in Canada. These consumers need to be not only informed but protected, for at the present time most of them are being victimized, beginning with all those who eat bread.
It is a known fact that in Canada, bread is made with wheat flour, from wheat considered the king of cereals. It is also known that wholesome and easily digestible bread should be made with whole wheat flour. But at present, that flour is reduced, then vitamin-enriched and even lime-enriched, because lime makes it easier to store flour, whereas regular flour is very difficult to store. Under the pretext of eliminating preservation problems, millers think they can do anything they like, even remove from wheat the most important, the most beneficial part for a normal digestion.
Lime can be used to paint a barn and will certainly do a good job. Lime can even be used to fertilize land, to make it more productive. But I do not think health benefits in any way from it. I do not believe it is beneficial for the people to eat bread to which lime has been added.
In the field of prepared meat, the same thing is true. Under the cover of the Food and Drugs Act, all kinds of operations are tried providing the results are not poisonous. The gimmick I would like to bring to your attention is used often enough throughout the year, but more so during the fall or the winter. I am referring to fresh minced pork
October 19, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs that is being sold to the customers, to the Canadian consumers. It is not mentioned very often because it is mostly poor people's meat, the meat of the small man, and when those people are involved it seems that anything goes. Right now, the common gimmick concerns everything called pork, all the fat of fresh pork meat which should normally be sold for the production of soap. Nowadays, butcher shops collect this pork, this fat, store it in freezers and, at the same time, store any red meat the colour of veal; all that too is frozen in large blocks of one foot by one foot by three feet and sold in the cities and throughout the rural areas as veal scrap. Such carrion, such hide-call it what you will- is sold at 35 cents a pound; to it is added the soap fat frozen by the butchers, and an average price of 50 cents a pound is arrived at for something costing 22 cents a pound.
As far as sausage meat is concerned, the same thing is true only more so. There again, no publication, no newspaper dares talk about the process because sausage is also the meat of the poor. Those products are prepared with ordinary meat, coloured to the highest degree, to which is added one part of soap fat, which I mentioned a minute ago, and corn meal. So, with 35 cents a pound for ordinary coloured meat, 10 cents a pound for soap fat and 8 cents a pound for corn meal, which makes 53 cents for three pounds, you have a product that is now sold $1.29 for three pounds-on special-which means a profit of 76 cents for the seller.
Mr. Speaker, under existing laws, it may be said without fear of contradiction that chickens are better protected in chickencoops than children in their own family, because when a poultryman buys a bag of chicken feed, a tag is affixed on the bag, showing the content in animal protein. And in the case I am referring to, there is no law that forces those people to indicate the composition of their product.
As a result, I hope that the new department will see that the housewife is shown the percentages of meal, soap-fat and flour contained in the meat she is buying at the butcher shop.
Great improvements are required with regard to labelling and I think that labels should state clearly the weight or the quantity as well as the quality, because that is not always the case at present. Standardization of containers should also be carried out so that the housewife can easily compare prices.


[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Today, whether we like it or not, information as to quality, variety and quantity is often greatly lacking. Several chain stores do not mention pounds, in fact not even ounces; they simply offer portions. Is it a morning, noon or evening portion? Is it a portion for a 51-pound child or for a 250-pound wrestler? At any rate, containers must be standardized.
In the directory distributed by the government two weeks ago, measures are mentioned, for instance. Quarts, and gallons are mentioned, in short we are told somewhat what is used in Canada. There too, we realize that fraud exists, because I remember for instance, that when my father was not yet known as a creditiste, when he was presented with a gallon of whiskey before election time, it was an Imperial gallon.
Today, when I purchase a gallon of antifreeze for my car, it is an Imperial gallon. But when my wife buys a gallon of fruit juice, it is an American gallon, and everyone knows that the American gallon contains three quarters of a quart less than the Canadian gallon.
So, all fruit juices now available to the Canadian housewife, whether orange, lemon or tomato juice, are sold in American measures when they come in gallon cans; however, these juices for sale in quarts are in Canadian measures, or Imperial quarts.
Moreover, children still learn in school that there are four quarts in one gallon, while the housekeeper still gets only 3| quarts for her gallon.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the new department will arrive at a standardization of containers and that when the housewife buys a gallon of fruit juice, she will get as much as the head of the family when he gets his gallon of whiskey.
The day before yesterday, the minister told us how much he wranted to help the small people. The previous speaker repeated what the minister said, that much needs to be done for those people.
They will be protected against bad salesmen and high interest rates, and I suppose it is very good to appear to protect them in that respect, but I have yet to see in the bill that the minister intends to protect them against taxes, indirect and hidden taxes, although they account for 25 per cent of the increase in the cost of living since 1960.
October 19, 1967

Does the new minister intend to disclose the secrets of the tax burden? Will he make public, for the benefit of the people, the many hidden taxes? Will the public finally get to know which taxes are paid by the manufacturer and which are paid by the retailer? Will it finally get to know about all the taxes imposed on buildings, about all the taxes charged here and there?
Since neither the miller, the baker, the grocer, the shop owner, the truck-driver, the railways nor the manufacturer ever pay taxes but just add those taxes to the price of their goods, we come to the conclusion that the only one who pay taxes are the people. Does the minister therefore intend to inform the people of the multiplicity of those hidden taxes and is he going to tell them through what kind of clever jugglery those taxes are collected?
As reported on page 3213 of Hansard, the minister also spoke of minority groups like those with low incomes who find it harder to make ends meet.
Well, let me tell the minister here that he should try to be better informed because if he wants to look after people with low incomes who can hardly make ends meet, he will find they are not a minority but the majority.
For his guidance the minister should read the May 5, 1967 issue of Travailleur cana-dien. In the city of Montreal-the minister may perhaps not be too well acquainted with that little corner of Quebec-where the threshold of poverty has been set at $2,250 per family, it is proved that 1,032,000 persons or 48.6 per cent of the total population in greater Montreal and the city itself, live in destitution, in extreme poverty or in want.
Had the threshold of poverty been set at $2,500 a year for a family of four, that percentage would be 68 per cent.
When the minister speaks of helping the small wage-earner I trust he will think of the 68 per cent of the population of the city of Montreal and all the others across the country.
Since it has been shown that taxes take up one third of our revenues, it is obvious that for low income workers, hidden taxes are much more costly than income tax.
Again, I hope the minister will warn the public; he will no doubt do so by saying: Dear citizens, we are protecting you against wolves and various monsters.
Corporate and Consumer Affairs
In reality, where are those wolves, those monsters? It is easy to say to manufacturers and dealers: we will protect you. But against what, against whom? In the manufacturing, wholesale and retail sectors, the governments' take is several times larger than that of corporations, in one fiscal area alone, such as sales tax.
Take for example the 11 per cent tax on building material. Since the wholesaler only gets a 3 per cent commission and the retailer only makes 5 per cent profit, this means that the two tradesmen who take care of the financing and transportation of these materials the two business concerns, the two associations and the two companies involved only make 8 per cent profit, while the government alone takes 11 per cent-not to mention the 8 per cent provincial tax which is added to all this.
The same happens with regard to car sales. About $800 must be paid in excise and federal sales tax on a car assembled in Sainte-Therese and sold for about $3,500 in Quebec. The 8 per cent provincial tax which is added to this amounts to about $300. This means that the federal and provincial governments together take in about $1,100 in tax while the salesman, who has to face competition and an uncertain future, has to make do with a small profit of only $125.
Fortunately, there are still some honest manufacturers and dealers who are conscientious and eager to serve their clients properly. It is useless to hope to serve a client properly when taxes account for a third of the bill.
Unless legislation is passed to remove 50 per cent of taxes, the creation of this department will lose 75 per cent of its effectiveness. The department may attempt to protect future home owners, by giving them some information on the quality of materials used, but it will be to no avail, the price of materials being prohibitive as a result of heavy taxes included in the price.
Recommendations may be made to prospective home owners, but they will be of no avail if the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will not make loans at an interest rate lower than 8j- per cent.
I wish to remind the government that it would be appropriate for the Bank of Canada to supply Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation with the funds needed in order to enable the C.M.H.C. to finance housing loans at a lower interest rate.

Corporate and Consumer Affairs [DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
At this stage, I am pleased to mention that the Creditistes are not the only ones to ask for a reform of the present system, and I want to quote from a brief presented by the Co-operative Council of Moncton to the joint committee on consumer credit at its sitting of March 21.
As recorded on page 2941 of No. 39, that association dares make recommendations to the government concerning the function of money and credit, and I quote:
In the field of trade, the function of money or credit should be to move goods or services. It should not be controlled as a commodity. Even now the chartered banks are largely bookkeeping institutions, and have the control of the creation of money or credit as a commodity which has tremendous influenoe in the business world and can set our interest rates. The cost of money or credit should not be more than the bookkeeping costs that are involved in keeping the records, but, when it is controlled as a commodity, it is used to restrict or expand the movement of goods at the will of those who control it for the purpose of making gain, and not solely for the purpose of servicing trade.
A little further, it is recommended in the brief:
That the Bank of Canada assume more control of the creation and distribution of needed credit (money).
The new department will be efficient, provided the consumer is in a position to consume and to pay for what he needs for his maintenance, which is not the case at the present time for large families. They should be the best consumers but to deserve that title they should receive family allowances three and even four times greater than what they are now, and as soon as possible.
The unemployed also are poor consumers at the present time. In order for them to get their share and to give them a place on the labour market, the government should lower the eligibility age for retirement pensions as soon as possible to make it available to all those people who have earned a well deserved rest after 40 and 45 years of hard work.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I wish the minister well in his new functions and, for his information and for the benefit of all the Canadian consumers, I recommend the perusal of No. 39 of the proceedings of the special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on consumer credit, especially the report of the sitting of Tuesday, March 21, 1967. I invite him to read this document over and over again because

DEBATES	October 19, 1967
he will find in it all the arguments and all the information necessary for a just and efficient administration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the measure now before the house represents the response of the government to increasing demands on the part of the general public for assistance in meeting some of the problems which face consumers in our country today.
It appears that the marketplace, like everything else, is becoming an ever more complex institution and those who make purchases are faced with a great many confusing situations. It is my belief that within this new department of government there will be ample opportunity for activities designed to meet a great many of the problems which face our people at the present time. If the government looks upon this new department solely as a means of quietening public protests, I suppose not very much will be achieved. On the other hands, if the new department is regarded as a means of meeting a very real challenge in our society, I believe many of the problems we face will be overcome and that in a number of ways the department will make an important contribution to the welfare and well-being of Canadian consumers.
There are many considerations which should occupy the attention of the new department if and when it is set up, and it appears to me that a number of these are of vital importance since they come so close to the consumer and have caused the consumer such concern and bewilderment, particularly in recent months. First, I should like to refer to the cost of living as we find it today. When we look at the charts we discover that the cost of living is constantly increasing. On the other side of the coin we find, of course, that there is a corresponding depreciation in the purchasing power of the dollar. This is causing our people a great deal of concern, unhappiness and in many cases hardship.
I do not intend today to discuss the effects of the cost of living in detail. This has been done on many occasions in the past. Indeed, whole debates in this house have been given over completely to discussion of this subject. But we have to remind ourselves that even though increases in pay have offset the effect of the rise in the cost of living for many of our citizens, there are still great numbers of people who are obliged to live on fixed incomes. These people, certainly, are caught in an economic squeeze.
October 19, 1967

We have heard on many occasions about the situation in which superannuated public servants find themselves. We are aware of the difficulties experienced by those who live on veterans allowances, disability pensions and other types of pensions. All these people are faced with an ever-increasing problem in procuring even the basic necessities of life. In some instances, at least, the government has seemed to be oblivious of this problem and its delay in seeking a solution is most disturbing to those involved.
I should like to refer to the promises which we have been given on many occasions in connection with possible increases in veterans pensions of various kinds. Whenever this question has been raised, and it has been on a number of occasions, the minister responsible has indicated that increases are under consideration but that because of delay in the completion of various reports it has not been possible so far to meet the demands of veterans organizations or those speaking on their behalf. On a number of occasions the minister has told us that if these reports were unduly delayed consideration would be given to the introduction of interim increases. He has told us this more than once, and the reply is now becoming monotonous since we all know that the reports have in fact taken far longer to complete than might reasonably be expected.
Hon. members have been told that the matter is under consideration. Meanwhile, these pensioners must continue to face an almost impossible situation in endeavouring to provide themselves with the necessities of life. In this area the minister responsible for this new department and his officials will have a job on their hands endeavouring to meet the needs of those who are directly affected by the increase in the cost of living which is taking place.
I should not like to take at face value statements which have been made to the effect that the federal government does not have jurisdiction or competence to deal with this problem. The constitutional limitations have been referred to today but I believe the minister and the government do have at their disposal some means of persuading those who are responsible for the price increases to take a careful look at their actions and endeavour to bring them more in line with reality and the requirements of our day. This is one thing which is very close to the hearts of the people since it affects the day to day living of all of us. For this reason I would urge the minister and the department, if and when it

Corporate and Consumer Affairs is set up, to give these matters prior consideration.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I should like to refer now to one of the recommendations of the special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, to be found on page 2184 of the committee proceedings. The committee recommends (a) that a department of consumer affairs, headed by a minister, be established and (b) that immediate steps be taken to promote standardization and simplification of grades, nomenclature and packaging for commonly purchased consumer items.
Here again we have a situation that is very confusing so far as the consumers are concerned. I would like to refer to a matter brought to my attention by one of my colleagues. He went into one store where he saw instant coffee advertised at a certain price. The product bore only one price. A short time later he went into another store and saw the same product labelled "30 cents off", yet its price in the second store was a little higher than the price in the first store. Consumers have great difficulty figuring out such things, and these are matters that should receive attention.
Packaging also gives rise to confusion. Reference was made this afternoon to the example of a large, beautifully coloured package of soap flakes which, when it was opened, was found to be only two-thirds filled with the product. A consumer looking at such a gigantic package in a store would think he was getting a good bargain but when he brought it home be would find very little of the product in it.

Corporate and Consumer Affairs been protected-the highest interest rates in the history of this country, the highest cost of living, the highest mortgage rate, up to 8J per cent, and on top of that the 11 per cent sales tax which falls on the consumer.
The government apparently has now had a little change of heart. Is it a change of heart or is it just a little window dressing? Today young couples cannot afford to buy their own homes. [DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The minister mentioned the low income consumer, the old age pensioner; and those who are receiving other social security benefits or pensions, all of whom must use their dollars effectively. Does the minister not realize that every new tax or tax increase imposed, no matter whether it is at the municipal, provincial or federal level, affects the purchasing power of the people of this country as much or more than some of the things such as price increases about which he spoke yesterday and the day before? The minister is adding personnel to the bureaucracy in establishing this new department. These additional people will have to be paid from taxes. I should like to ask the government what is wrong in this country today. Canadians are today buying more securities from foreign sources than ever before. They do not believe our management is good enough. In one month alone $45 million more securities were bought in Canada from the United States than were bought from Canada by the United States. And we must remember that the population of the United States is ten times that of this country.
I hope the government realizes the very serious position in which they are putting us. No country in the world today has the natural resources per capita that Canada has. Our natural resources per capita are much greater than those of the United States. This government needs top-level management. We do not need so many commissions or departments but rather top-level management.
The Economic Council of Canada has indicated that the government is a pretty bad spender. Perhaps this was the reason the government decided to appoint a minister to look after consumer affairs. If that was the reason, perhaps they have hit on something for the first time. If anyone thinks that we do not need consumer protection in this country and control over the money the government spends, let him consider the situation in Canada against that of a comparable country.

Let us examine the period from 1963 to 1966 when this government was in power. We find that in this period public spending in the United States rose by only 25 per cent. In Canada public spending rose by 35 per cent in the same period. There is a differential of 10 per cent, and it is a good indication that we need somebody to protect the consumer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
Perhaps I am making the minister's job more solid because I have indicated that we need him. We badly need somebody to watch the spending of the government. I hope the minister will take these remarks in good spirit because I really mean what I am saying. It is also interesting to note that this government collects approximately twice as much in income tax as was collected in 1961. This is the No. 1 reason why the consuming public requires protection. I hope the minister will give top priority to this aspect of his responsibilities.
Let us consider the situation of the consumer who purchased 3 per cent perpetual government bonds in 1937. I can see by the minister's expression that he knows what I am coming to. I do not know whether he has looked at the record, but I would tell him that today those bonds are bid at 47 cents on the dollar. If there is one thing that can create an aura of dishonesty and default in this country, it is when government bonds are bid at 47 cents on the dollar.
The minister could tell his colleagues in the cabinet that this situation might come under the heading of fraud and deception,
Corporate and Consumer Affairs which is one of the matters he will be investigating. We look forward to seeing that these bonds are paid for pretty promptly when the minister assumes his new responsibilities. I hope I do not have to remind the minister that in 1961 the Conservative government had a positive trade balance and today we have a trade deficit of over $750 million.
I notice also that four fields of government activity were classified by the Economic Council of Canada as being fields which should be investigated. The first was protection against fraud and deception; second, protection of health and safety; third, protection of products standards and grades; and fourth, preparing consumer information. This is a large field, and dozens of provincial and municipal governments across the country are now licensing and legislating in these areas.
What is the minister going to do about consumer credit? A great deal of consumer credit is now under provincial control. Will this department be another bureaucracy created to make people think the government is doing something, when in the long run it will mean they will be saddled with the expense of another bureaucratic department? Could not all these things have been accomplished by the Registrar General (Mr. Turner)? I believe we all have quite an admiration for the Registrar General, this young man from Montreal. I think he is a likeable fellow. I just wonder whether he as Registrar General could not have accomplished every solitary thing that he says he will accomplish in this new portfolio.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
In financial affairs there is no difference between the government and the people from whom it collects taxes except that it has a little more collateral. This year the government will still have to find, after it has sold its Canada savings bonds, $300 million or $400 million of new money with which to meet its present commitments. I do not say this in a partisan spirit or in a spirit of antagonism. What I am saying is that we are in a bad situation and it is about time we started to get down to brass tacks and to think of the Canadian consumer and the Canadian taxpayer, the little fellow who is making Canada and keeping the wheels turning. I say this in all sincerity.
Further, I should like to know what tinkering the minister proposes with the patent laws, particularly as they affect drugs. We must remember the general principle that if all imports were allowed to enter Canada
3278	COMMONS
Corporate and Consumer Affairs free of tariff we would have little secondary industry in this country. There are certain reasons for this but I do not intend to go into them at this time. The Economic Council of Canada sounded a warning in this regard in its interim report. I hope the minister has read it.
If the minister does tinker with the patent laws concerning drugs, how many people is he going to throw out of work? Will it be 2,000, 5,000 or 10,000? In the last few days we have all been gravely concerned, as we should be, about the 3,000 people in Nova Scotia who may lose their jobs. I hope measures will be taken by the government to see that a solution is reached which will enable these people to continue working.
I wonder whether the minister knows that Mr. Henry-I am sure he knows Mr. Henry very well-who proposed the changes in the patent and trade mark legislation to the Harley committee, based them on the assumption that we could get along very well without a drug industry in Canada. I hope the minister understands that because it is a very important point. Before the minister changes the patent and trade mark laws, will he indicate to the house how many firms might well close up shop in Canada and manufacture in the U.S.A. where productivity is about one third higher per worker or, for that matter, manufacture drugs in European countries where labour costs are lower? If these companies did move out and we imported our supplies, what would become of the nearly 3,000 university graduates who work in the industry in Canada, each of whom has cost the taxpayers a great deal of money from the baby bonus onward and represents at 30 years of age a potential earning capacity of nearly $1.5 million to the country to which he might go?
Do we give up our own research and depend on some other country, or will we be stuck with paying through the nose to the country that does our research in lifesaving drugs which are not in common use but are needed occasionally? I wonder how much this will increase our already unfavourable trade balance? However, I will not pursue this subject further at the present time as there are several other matters which can be explored. My only desire is the safest of drugs at satisfactory prices.
About 50 years ago 60 per cent of the retail sales were made either on a cash basis or on a credit basis with accounts payable at the end of the month. Today we operate on a basis of 60 per cent credit or more. Some of

DEBATES	October 19, 1967
these sales are made on revolving credit accounts whereby we establish credit for the articles we want to buy and make monthly payments thereafter. If the payments are kept up one may from time to time make additional purchases on the same account. What are the finance charges under this credit arrangement? I wonder whether the minister can tell us. Does the buyer know and does the government know what these charges are?
About 50 years ago one could obtain a cash discount. Today there are no cash discounts. We buy on credit more often from companies which can establish their own credit terms if and when they require them, sometimes at 6 per cent on the present market. These companies are often large outfits which use this money to make loans and in this way make money on money. It is only fair to say that the administration costs must be taken out of the 12 per cent profit. It is also only fair to say that once a person obtains a revolving credit account he tends to continue buying from that company without shopping around and he often pays prices which he would not pay if he were able to compare prices and had not established that line of credit.
Would the minister give us an idea as to what he proposes to do in this regard? Are the largest department stores going to be allowed to run their own credit business as they like? What is to be done with the finance companies which have gone into the car rental business and have cut into car sales? Should supply and demand rule here? What is to be done with regard to those companies which build homes and sell them completely furnished? They are interfering with the furnishing business and with the suppliers of electrical equipment. How is the small businessman to be helped in order to compete?
We know that the use of money must be paid for, but this was not always the case. At one time the collecting of interest was an offence. It was not until the sixteenth century that interest became an accepted fact and it is only in the present century that consumer credit became a fact of life. Consumer credit is profitable in many cases and keeps the economy moving. It is a service to many young people who wish to get married and acquire the necessary household effects. It is an accepted method of conducting business. However, it happens quite often that the consumer buys where he has established credit without checking or comparing prices.
October 19, 1967

In many instances he does not have the incentive to shop in other stores for bargain sales which are often held during certain seasons of the year. A justification will have to be made for the establishment of this department.
I should now like to go on to the subject of advertising. 1 am particularly concerned about this field. Today a question was asked in the house with regard to cigarette smoking. Cigarette brands are being advertised extensively. We hear about long cigarettes and long filters. We are told this is the cool cigarette, this is the right smoke, one that gives you a lift. What are we doing about it? The department of the Minister of National Health and Welfare has done a little work on this subject in the last three or four years ever since this matter was brought up in the house. I should like to ask the minister what his ideas are on that subject and what is he going to do about it. If anything is needed to spur him on, it is this article which appeared in today's Globe and Mail, part of which reads as follows:
A Toronto surgeon who has made a study of lung cancer, yesterday accused the tobacco industry of "callous disregard of public safety" in introduction of the 100-millimetre cigaret.
Dr. Norman C. Delarue, assistant professor of surgery at the University of Toronto, said this action focused clear light upon the industry's intent: the long cigaret was purely a sales gimmick.
Dr. Delarue told the closing session of the annual meeting of the Ontario Chapter of the College of General Practice of Canada that government, industry and physicians should take certain steps.
I hope the minister will listen carefully to what I have to say now because it is important. I believe the government should immediately outlaw 100-millimetre cigarettes and should set the maximum tar content of cigarettes at 15 milligrammes and the maximum nicotine content at 1.6 milligrammes. It should also insist on more straightforward labelling. I wonder what we will have to do to stir the government out of its apathy and get some action.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I want to say that I believe that now we have this young, ambitious minister he may be able to find solutions to some of these problems. I say that again in all sincerity. He and I have been friends ever since he came into this house. I have admired him and his capabilities. But I was a little bit ashamed the other day when we had to listen to him for an hour and forty minutes saying nothing. He really let me down. Nevertheless, I do like him and I think he is generally liked.
Corporate and Consumer Affairs
If we need to add to this evidence, Mr. Speaker, we can cite the fact that the directors of the American Cancer Society have recommended that cigarette advertising be ended. I want to tell the minister that this is his cue. Let him act right away. Let him make a name for himself by ending the advertising of cigarettes right now. It is stated that advertising is too persuasive, too valid and too vital a part of the life of the American continent to be used in the sale of such a lethal product as the cigarette. This, Mr. Speaker, is the key to the whole problem. If the minister listens, if he catches on, he will immediately start to work with his colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) to put an end to this advertising. We have to stop this nefarious trade. In another article, in the Gazette for October 16, 1967, it is stated that the death rate has been cut down but the number of lung cancers in women is increasing as the effects of cigarette smoking are being felt.
I should like to conclude by saying that the minister will justify the establishment of this department only if he proves to us he is doing something for the working people of this country. He will have to prove that he is sincere in what he is doing. I hope he will not end up, as the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) said, sitting in his goldplated Cadillac. We would not like to see this handsome young man-he has been blessed with good looks-sitting in his goldplated Cadillac with no gas in it. We would not like to see him, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam (Mr. Douglas) said, riding that old winded horse. I am sure none of us wants these things to befall the minister. All of us wish him the very best, but when I heard that hour and 40 minute speech I could not help but think of those words of Oliver Goldsmith, I believe, which I will paraphrase this way: "As on and on he went, the wonder grew how one small head could carry all he knew." As I said before, I have high regard for the minister. I hope he will not let us down and I wish him the very best in his department.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us deals with the establishment of a department of corporate and consumer affairs.
We note in reading section 6, that one of the main purposes of that department will be to promote the interests of the consumers, to protect them and see to it that they are
3280	COMMONS
Corporate and Consumer Affairs better informed. Certainly everyone approves and commends all these objectives because everyone is of the opinion that the government must do everything in its power to ensure better protection for the Canadian consumer.
When General Eisenhower was still in Europe and he was approached and offered the candidacy of the Republican party in the United States, reporters asked him: What do you think of the rise in the cost of living? Do you think that citizens accept it? Do you think that it is normal? And General Eisenhower replied: When my wife comes back from shopping, she feels that the cost of living is increasing and that it costs a lot to live today.
That was many years ago and today we are still faced with the same problems. But the government has decided to set up a department which will deal specifically with ways to improve the lot of all Canadians.
The problem of protecting the consumer is not simple and easy to solve. In fact, it is an extremely complex problem, which has ramifications in practically all sectors of the economy, and it is of course a problem which creates a lot of interest since the ordinary citizen has each day the opportunity to realize its implications.
Everyone agrees on the objectives the government has set itself but some parties obviously disagree about the ways to achieve more successfully the objectives sought.
The Conservative party has made known its official policy through its spokesman, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) who, during his whole speech, has maintained that the minister's powers were inadequate-they should be increased and should have more teeth. He made his point so well that one wonders if the Conservative party has not initiated a new policy, if it is not drifting towards direct price control as was done in wartime.
And I should like to quote part of the speech delivered by the official spokesman for the Conservative party. As it is recorded in Hansard, on page 3239, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) said:

The government Is going to try to persuade everybody in a friendly fashion to toe the line. That is all the minister can do under this bill. He can cajole, threaten and persuade, but he cannot enforce. The legislation has no teeth.

DEBATES	October 19, 1967
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)

This is proof that the Conservative party through its official spokesman would like the government, if not directly at least indirectly, to implement a price control policy.
Is it the result of the last convention? Would the official leader of the Conservative party be ready to support his spokesman in the house and state that he unreservedly approves his policy? Is it really the new policy of the Conservative party? This is still doubtful and the answers are yet to come.
While the same hon. member says that the bill does not contain sufficient power and that the government will fail to attain its objectives, he adds that it is absolutely useless to increase the number of officials and to increase expenses to achieve the government's purpose.
What does the Conservative party want exactly? Does it want legislation giving broader powers but without providing the required staff to implement it? Does the Conservative party want to resort to political expediency? Does it simply wish to throw a smoke screen? This would be quite consistent with the new image of the Conservative party. This would reflect exactly the policy of Mr. Camp when he told the Canadian people: We must put an end to all our military alliances. And in the next paragraph, but with much less emphasis he added: That program could be carried out over a ten-year period.
This is exactly the same policy now being advocated by the Conservative party, when they say: We want the government to have much broader powers, but not the staff to administer the department, to support the minister.
It is an inconsistent policy and, surely, the people of Canada will not accept it gratuitously and without discussion.
As for the N.D.P., by repeated references to the fact that they do now want to revert to wartime and pursue a policy of direct price control, they lead us to believe, although indirectly, that the government should have had a price control policy.
Why not come out with it if a direct price control is being advocated? Why beat around the bush and suggest to the people that something should be avoided but that nevertheless every means should be employed to achieve it?
This is still an expedient lacking frankness and realism.
October 19, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs increased tariffs, because of the adverse effects of undue competition, mainly from Japan, to the extent that 50 per cent of the shoes sold in Canada last year originated from foreign countries.
Now, does the hon. member for Yukon suggest that Canada, by rejecting overnight all tariff limitations, would better protect the consumer? Would such a solution help the consumer? Rather, would it not create unemployment in Canada? Would it solve the problem, to bring overnight the whole industry to the brink of bankruptcy?
In other words, consumer problems need and will continue to require concerted effort on the part of several departments. That is why it is clearly stated in the bill, among the powers stipulated, that the new department will have to co-ordinate the activity of several departments in this field because one department alone would never have all the powers necessary to protect the consumer adequately.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the new department will fulfill its duties splendidly. But, once again, we Canadian citizens should not depend entirely on the government. The consumer should strive to be better informed and to protect himself better. This is one of the very important tasks of the present government. It could not assume all responsibility for the Canadian people in this field. It must keep the consumer well informed so that the latter will know what he buys, how to buy and the quality of the goods he buys.
It is most important-it is our civic duty as parliamentarians in this country-that we make the citizens realize their own duty, their own responsibility. It seems to me that leaving everything to the government is a very easy way to solve the problems of Canada.
On the contrary, we should appeal to the understanding and the good sense of the citizens. If the minister could at a very early date, achieve a nation-wide public information policy, which would give the country complete and accurate information, a lot would have been achieved for Canada because we are not the only country having to face tremendous problems as far as consumers are concerned.
Once again I quote the Economic Council of Canada report which stated, in its conclusion:
It is clear from the experience of other countries that there are many methods of dealing with problems in the consumer field, and that a flexible

approach emphasizing effective solutions would be more appropriate than one characterized by rigidities and doctrinaire formulas.
Such is government policy, in short such is the challenge to the new minister and I am sure he will take it up.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on the bill. I have been interested in the statements that have been made, particularly by the hon. members for Yukon (Mr. Nielson) and Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard). There is no point in my repeating what they said as they expressed themselves more clearly on the subject than I could hope to.
I wished to speak about finance, retail credit, interest charges and related matters. As the hon. member for Simcoe East also dealt with such matters thoroughly I need not go to great lengths to repeat what was said. I am interested in Bill C-161, to establish a department of corporate and consumer affairs. I am in favour of establishing the department if it will do some of the things we expect of it. We hope it will render a genuine service to the consumer and, in a proper sense, protect him. The consumer today, as never before, needs protecting. Some may say that the bill will protect consumers against themselves. I do not hold with such thinking.
I could support this bill wholeheartedly if the department which it will create could check inflation. Inflation is not easily cured and it is not sensible for us to expect the new minister or the new department to cure it. That is not within the bounds of possibility. Nevertheless, if the new department could in some way prevent the ever-increasing upward spiral of food prices, hold food prices in check and help those who own or rent homes by keeping the costs they have to meet within reasonable bounds, we should all be grateful. I contend that the moneys paid out by consumers for groceries and rent represent the greatest expenditures that they must meet today.
I had the privilege of being on the committee that dealt with consumer credit from the day of its inception. I attended almost all the committee meetings and I wish to pay tribute to the chairmen of the committee, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Bas-ford) and Senator Croll, two dedicated men who took their task most seriously. I do not believe that the bill now before the house
October 19, 1967

contains in its provisions the recommendations of that committee.
I wish to raise a point and ask the minister what he intends to do for the individual food processor. Since the matter may be difficult to follow, may I cite an example. I suggest that the minister and his department will wish to inquire more deeply into the subject matter I am about to raise. I know of a food processor in eastern Canada who for many years supplied the large food chains with many items of food that were sold under their private labels. Eventually he decided that he would introduce his own brand of product under his own private label. The big chain stores thereupon informed him that he must pay for the right to display his merchandise in their stores.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
This processor was told it would cost him $2,500 before his merchandise would be displayed. He was further told it would cost him a certain amount of money to support an advertising program. They would not guarantee him anything. They would order certain amounts of merchandise in lots to be delivered if, as and when they decided they wanted them. They made various other requests of him. This man said he would not go along. They said: "That is all right; we will discontinue ordering your merchandise. As a result, his merchandise was not displayed. He was in a position where he found himself being squeezed out of business by these large firms. I should like to know what the minister intends to do about this type of blackmail. He does not need to look far to find a concrete case. I refer to a firm known or formerly known as Pyramid Canners; some of these people may still be around. I understand they were squeezed out of business in this manner.
Let us consider the price maintenance factor. I know that some people will say: We do not have price maintenance any more. I think we do. Take, for instance, a large firm-I will not mention names-which has what I would call its own stencil line. It is selling this line at its own price. It can establish whatever price it wishes on this line because it is not available to any other retailer; none of the other retailers or merchandisers can purchase this line because the factories which manufacture it are owned by this large interest. The company can therefore establish whatever price it wishes. This, I contend, is price maintenance. I could enlarge on this and mention many different items which the company sells using this
Corporate and Consumer Affairs system. I do not think it is fair to the consumer. This is a matter which I am sure the new department will wish to consider thoroughly.
I should like to turn for a moment to a report which has often been quoted in the house, the interim report by the economic council on consumer affairs to the Department of the Registrar General. On page 20 we find the following:
In view of the wide scope of consumer interests and the many departments which are engaged in activities affecting consumers, there is no possibility of concentrating all these activities in a single department, nor would it be desirable to try to do so. A great improvement in present methods of co-ordination is necessary, however, and for this purpose we recommend the establishment of an interdepartmental committee on consumer affairs under the chairmanship of the Deputy Registrar General. The committee should include the Deputy Ministers of Trade and Commerce, National Health and Welfare, Industry, Agriculture, Fisheries, Insurance, Finance and Justice, and such other departments as have a continuing interest in consumer matters. In such matters as food, pesticides, consumer credit, consumer goods standards and trade practices, where responsibilities are widely distributed, such co-ordination is imperative for efficient administration. This committee should have a permanent secretariat within the Department of the Registrar General which would assist in the work of the committee and in keeping the minister informed of federal government activities in the field of consumer affairs.
My contention is that since each of these different departments is responsible for certain facets of consumer affairs the minister should recruit his staff by transferring personnel, with their co-operation, to the new department of corporate and consumer affairs. I should like to quote the minister's words as reported in Hansard on October 13. He said then:
Mr. Chairman, the aim of this legislation is to promote co-ordination in the field of consumer affairs. In the past, the activities of the federal government with regard to the protection or information of consumers were divided between several departments, that is to say there never was any co-ordinated program or, if I may be allowed to use that term, any appeal court for the consumers who wanted help or information from the federal government.
The minister went on to speak very constructively, I thought, on this subject. I contend that people could be transferred to the new department from the Department of Industry. I am concerned about this mushrooming of departments. The Department of Industry was established some four years ago and today it has 783 employees. Many of the things now being done by the Department of Industry will be handled in future by the new department of consumer affairs. Aspects
3284	COMMONS
Corporate and Consumer Affairs of the work now carried on by the Department of Trade and Commerce are also involved. The same could be said about some of the work now done by the Department of Agriculture and the Department of National Health and Welfare. Many of the staff presently employed in those departments should be brought under the umbrella of the new ministry.
Let us simply transfer these people. Let us not hire new staff. We have gone far enough in that direction already and I think it is time we got away from this empire building tendency. I do not see how we can afford it any more. I think we should get away from this idea of government by bureaucracy. In 1939 there were some 30,000 employees in the public service. Today, according to the figures I have, there are 372,890. It just does not make sense that there should be more than ten times as many public employees today as there were 30 years ago. I know the people cannot afford it. I know we cannot afford an expensive type of government like this any longer.
I would refer hon. members to an item which appeared in the Globe and Mail yesterday. It reads as follows:
A strongly worded criticism of government monetary and fiscal policy by Neil J. McKinnon, chairman of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, was delivered yesterday to an international conference of the Financial Executives Institute.
Mr. McKinnon warned that an increasing rate of inflation only could end up causing a painful readjustment in the economy.
"All experience in history has shown that inflationary trends, from whatever source they may arise, if not firmly checked, lead to serious harm to the great mass of people including all of those whom government spending programs of various kinds are intended to benefit."
The chief executive officer of Canada's second largest chartered bank wasted little time in identifying the source of Canada's inflationary problems.
"The fall in the value of money always stems from continuous government deficits, especially those in time of high employment, accompanied by an increase in money supply which tends to monetize at least part of the deficits."
It is not too much to say that government deficit spending, combined with a permissive monetary policy that allows continuous inflation really involve a massive swindle-a swindle perpetrated on the great majority of the populace who are least able to protect themselves against the consequences.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Farther on he quoted Bernard Baruch as follows:
"People who talk about gradually inflating might as well talk about firing off a gun gradually."
Very pertinently I would like to ask the minister what will this new department do

DEBATES	October 19, 1967
that might, and I emphasize might, control inflation? Where are the teeth in this bill? I see nothing set out as penalties. What are the minister's plans? How can this new ministry render a service and be of service to the consumer? What exactly will this new department offer?
Let us consider weights and measures which are important so far as the consumer is concerned. What will this new department do that is not now being done by the weights and measures branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce? What will the new department do in the important field of retail inspection that is not already being done by the appropriate agency under the Department of Trade and Commerce? What will it do so far as deceptive and restrictive trade practices are concerned, matters which are now handled by the Department of Justice and other departments? What will it do in connection with food and drugs? These are things which were touched on this afternoon. In connection with food and drugs what will the new department do that is not already being done by the Department of National Health and Welfare?
I hope we will receive answers to some of these questions. I am very interested in these matters. I think everyone in the house should be interested in them because they have to do with the general welfare and well-being of our country. I would like to support this bill but first I want to know how the proposed bill will assist the consumer.

I am sure they will take their direction from him instead of vice-versa. We must break the evils of corporate structures today and some of the very rotten foundations which underlie them. We still have some good companies, and I am speaking of public as well as private companies. There are also problems of financing, but I will not deal with those at the moment.
As I have said these companies have lost their continuity of ownership and indeed the directors and shareholders of a corporation today really are not interested in the production of that company. One would be amazed at the number of directors of large corporations who are really interested in whether or not the company makes a profit or has a good product. They are, however, very interested in any avenue by which they can romance-if that is the right word-the shares so they can make money on the sale of the shares. Ownership of the corporation is merely a method of gambling. It is difficult for management and labour to find any incentive to do a good job, because who cares when this attitude on the part of the directors is known. I have looked at the record of the directors of several corporations. They do not receive very much in directors' fees. Indeed, $500 a year or something of this nature is being paid to directors of five or six companies. It always amazes me how they can drive large Cadillacs and live in such a luxurious manner. Surely they are not doing it on $500 a year.
The rights to subscribe for new issues of shares are handed down from father to son and from uncle to nephew. These rights to buy shares are placed on the market. The directors do not issue the shares until they
[Mr. Otto.l

have made money on the rights. The emphasis is not on whether the company has conducted an honourable business but rather on how they can sell the shares to make a buck. This, of course, corrupts all business. These are the problems we must face. A recent and perfect example of this, of which all members are aware, is the great Atlantic fiasco. I do not think there is any other set of circumstances which so clearly explains the play of share take-overs. No product was involved in this whole thing, so it could not be said there was a good product which was making money. A well-established man could walk into any bank and say, "Buy some of these shares; they are a good thing." The reason for a take-over is not to make a company more successful. Take-overs or amalgamations are merely for the purposes of enhancing, either fictiously or otherwise, the value of shares in order to make a dollar for the large shareholder.
Surely I need not go further than to say that when this situation exists among the owners of shares it is difficult to avoid corruption or ensure that the business will be conducted in an honourable way. How can these evils which are evident today be avoided? The most one can do is to pass a law. We may say that they cannot do this, but they will do it in another way. I think the root of the problem is the whole corporate structure and I believe that with revision and reform of the corporate structure we might expect some improvement in competition.
In line with this, and as a complementary thing, we have the structure of our stock exchanges. About a year ago, I believe, the minister pinpointed some of the problems which exist as a result of each province having its own stock exchange. I believe this speech was made in New York, although I do not remember now. However, this is a great problem because the one complements the other. Any hon. member who has had experience in trying to put stock on the public market will know what the cost of such a promotion is. It is amazing.

When he spoke earlier about his views as to why there is some undue exploitation of the consumer-the words are his-he left the impression he felt if there was undue exploitation it was caused by some process of decay in corporate structure.
I must admit that I did not take prolific notes. I cannot recall precisely the words he used, but he left the impression with me, at least, that he felt the problem resulted from a process within corporate organization whereby management was going more and more into the hands of people who have no direct interest; that ownership is not concerned with the ethics of the business operation but concerned almost exclusively with the profit that can be made from dealing with shares. If I have not quoted the hon. member accurately, I apologize, but I believe a reading of the record tomorrow will bear me out.
If the hon. member really meant what he said, I am surprised. This process has been
