going on during the entire post-war period. In fact, it could be seen at work as early as 1920. Therefore, if we have problems in the field of consumer affairs, the undue exploitation of consumers to use the hon. member's own words, these problems result from a process which has been at work for several decades. It is time we came to grips more tangibly with this problem than we have up to now.
I want to say to the minister that I should like very much to compliment him on quite a few things. I desist from doing so, since he has received so many compliments already from the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) and the hon. member for York East. We must not forget the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), because I believe some of his remarks were meant to be complimentary.
I wish I might say something positive about this government and its actions to date in respect of protecting the consumer in the marketplace and in connection with the borrowing of money. Only a few days ago this government did proclaim regulations requiring the full disclosure of interest rates both in the absolute amount and in a percentage rate sense as well. I believe that this will do some good by way of protecting the consumer from abuses. This is positive action, Mr. Speaker, and I refer to it in order to point out something else, that is that this government has shown in the last few days that there are two ways of going about tampering with a serious problem. One way is to step in and deal with the problem with a minimum of fanfare, proposing legislation or proclaiming regulations, thus getting the job done. This is the course the government took in respect of the disclosure of interest rates, for which most members would give them credit.
The other way of tackling a problem is the course the government has adopted in respect of consumer affairs generally. Instead of setting to and grappling with it without too much fanfare, they are doing just the opposite. They are giving the appearance of wrestling with the problem, when in fact they are only fussing with form, fussing with organization and really doing nothing new at all about the substance of the problem. There has been, I feel, sufficient reference already to just how the legislation before us will not be very effective, will not serve the consumer's interest in the marketplace.
The bill before us is to establish a department of corporate and consumer affairs. Members on my right from the Conservative
October 19, 1967

party have been referring to it as an indication of more red tape being served up by this government. Some of my colleagues have referred to this bill as window dressing. I think they are both right. This government is dressing its windows with red tape. They hope to create the impression amongst the general public that they are really determined now, in 1967, to pass meaningful legislation that will stop some of the abuses currently existing in our business life. If this is the intention of the government, I fail to see where it is being given legislative effect. The only part of the bill which deals with the powers of this new department of corporate and consumer affairs is clause 6, and it does not specify in any concrete way just what the government will do that is new in the field of consumer legislation.
I do not apologize to the hon. member for York East when I say that I would be enthused about the prospect of establishing a department of consumer affairs if I could be assured that accompanying that there would be recommended to this house legislation that would have some teeth in it. I know that in the past the federal government, as well as the present minister who will head this department, have stated time and time again there is a constitutional problem resulting from the division of powers. Almost everyone realizes that today. At the same time, as the minister said, the general public to use the minister's expression are becoming more educated, and therefore they expect more from government in the way of meaningful consumer legislation. If it is not forthcoming they will expect this impasse which has been caused by the constitutional division of powers to be solved somehow. The minister said that the people of Canada expect governments these days to organize themselves in a better way. He is certainly right. This is the feeling I have as well. If the people expect governments to organize themselves better, it follows they will expect governments to organize better in the sense that they can close the gap of the constitutional no man's land that has existed between the two levels of government from 1867 until now. Mr. Speaker, in rising to address the house in respect of this bill to establish a department of corporate and consumer affairs, first of all I should like to
Corporate and Consumer Affairs congratulate the minister upon his accepting this portfolio. I have noticed during this debate that hon. members of other parties have also extended their good wishes.
This will be a challenging department. It has been said here that probably there is legislation which is administered by other departments which covers areas which will be covered by this new department. However, unlike some of the members who have spoken and have looked back, I should like to say that I believe it is more important that we should look forward. I believe this new department is a forward looking department and has a forward looking minister.
The problems of the consumers today will not be solved by looking backward; they will be solved by looking ahead. The objectives contained in this bill cover several areas. One objective is that the consumer will be given a voice, through committees or through advisers to the government, in respect of matters affecting him. Another aim of the bill is, by legislation, research and education, to improve the quality of consumer demand and thereby place him in a better position to evaluate the products on which he is spending his income. It will also provide orderly channelling of consumer submissions and inquiries. One of the functions of this department will be to work with the provinces on the problems of the consumer.
It would be ideal if by simple legislation we could achieve the direct result of legislating on the price of every single item on which every person in this country spends money. I do not believe, however, that even the most vehement objectors to the contents of this bill would suggest that this is possible. It is neither possible nor desirable. But it is desirable that the consumer should be able to spend his or her income in the most effective way. The bill is entitled, "An act to establish a department of corporate and consumer affairs." I think the name "corporate and consumer affairs" is good. I believe it is most important that we endeavour to help the consumer. I also think that one should not attempt to segregate the consumer and the corporation. When the consumer spends his or her dollar it goes to someone else, and the consumer receives something in return. We hope to see that the consumer receives better value.
It is hoped that this department will be able to better educate the members of the public in respect of their buying. When I say it in that way, it sounds very simple, but it is not something which can be legislated easily.

Corporate and Consumer Affairs AH members of this house of course are consumers. Some of us are knowledgeable about some items we all buy and others are knowledgeable about other items. Even if we take the example of a simple item like a package of soap, it is difficult to say how far one can go in evaluating what is contained in the package. Do you evaluate its capacity to clean or its ability to work in hard water or soft water? The actual weight of the contents by volume can be printed on the package. You can give a realistic evaluation of the size of this item, but you cannot evaluate its full chemical ability.

It is hoped that this department will also be able to combat the practice of price fixing whereby a price is agreed upon by various manufacturers so that there is no competition with respect to the product. The most important function the department will have, as far as the consumers of Canada are concerned, is that it will release the competitive forces among various manufacturers and suppliers, because the bases upon which we operate are competition and fair selling practices. I hope the department will investigate the problems inherent in some of our service stations. I refer to what amounts almost to an impossibility in some areas for service stations to operate unless they are franchised by one of the major suppliers of oil, gasoline and oil products.
We also have monopolistic monsters in the form of chain stores and chain groceries. While we cannot claim that they have a complete comer on the market, at least not in the big cities because there are various chains, they do have control in that they are beginning to own the supply house for the supermarket as well as the retail operation. While they compete strongly in certain items that they advertise heavily and display prominently, there are other basic, stock items carried in these stores with regard to which, by keeping a close eye on other chains, the price is not as competitive as it might otherwise be.
There is another area that I hope this department will look into. I refer to the lending houses which lend large and small amounts of money at what would appear to be a high rate of interest that is not always well identified. I believe this situation is being corrected so that the individual borrower will be able to evaluate the interest charged on his loan.

Many of the problems facing the consumer today are caused by our prosperity. They are the problems inherent in a high standard of living and in the fact that we now expect to have more and to live better, as we should. We have these problems, and we welcome them. But we also have the problems of poverty, to a lesser degree, in our smaller areas. These are problems which it is hoped the new department will combat. I believe the department will combat them effectively.
I am pleased to learn that the new department will have control in the area of bankruptcy. In this field the department will be working closely with the R.C.M.P., which is so effective in many areas. Working with the R.C.M.P. in bankruptcy matters will I am sure assist the department to be extremely effective.
Bankruptcies will of course occur. However, when a bankruptcy occurs the consumer still pays, because the end result of the operation of any company is to make a profit, and the figures in the bottom right-hand corner of the balance sheet show this profit. Profit is the end result of any company. If a company does not make profit, it will not stay in business. If the creditors of a company do not pay their bills, the company must make its basic profit or at least break even, otherwise it goes out of business. The result of a company going out of business comes back to the consumer just like the wave from a stone thrown into a pond.
We are told that this new department will hear from task forces which will consult experts from the business and academic worlds. These task forces will supply ideas to the department and keep it informed of the latest developments in the economic world. I believe this is an important function of the department of the future, because consumer affairs are a reflection of what is happening to each and every person in Canada today.
As the world around us changes, so must the forces affecting the consumer change. It will not do to establish a department and say: This is good; we now have the solution. We do have a method of seeking the solution today, and I am pleased to know that the department will seek advice and will keep in contact with the consumer. It is comforting to know that the department will receive fresh ideas from people outside the department. In this way this department of the future will not be allowed to become stale.
The department will also be concerned, in co-operation with other departments, in the establishment of fair weights and measures.

It is perhaps difficult to establish a system of fair weights and measures and lay down firm rules and say: This is what you will do. I do not think that in our society you can say: You must pack peas in a quart can; you must pack carrots in a pint can. But you can ensure that weights are properly shown and identified in terms that the consumer can understand. I think this will be done.
In some areas, particularly in the area of advertising, there are problems which I hope this department will attack. It is simple to say that the major cost of any retail items is the advertising that the manufacturer and the supplier undertake. The money the manufacturer or supplier spends on advertising always goes into the cost of the product and is paid by the consumer. I do not think we can say legislatively that there will be no more advertising. I do not believe this would be fair.
I do not think this sort of approach would be a proper one in our society, and it is not realistic. I say this because there are several factors involved in the cost of an item. One of the major factors is volume. Advertising makes a product known, particularly a new product. Through advertising, the product sells. If it sells in volume, it can be sold to the consumer at a lower price. It is therefore difficult to say whether advertising is suitable or excessive.
I think we all know that when a new product comes on the market, the manufacturer expects to lose money at the start of his operation. He expects to lose money because at the start of the operation he has to undertake more advertising and he also has a very small volume. As volume builds up and advertising comes down, the price becomes more realistic.

I find it irritating, to say the least-although I am not a great follower of contests-to pick up a magazine that is sold in Canada and that advertises a product sold in Canada, and read an advertisement of a contest to give away a new car or a television set or offering a trip to a distant point with a companion of your choice, and then read in the bottom line of this advertisement that the prize is not available to residents other than those of our great neighbour to the south, the United States. Corporate and Consumer Affairs there are to be contests-contests are good things because many people enjoy them and there are even some who win-then I think the winners should be allowed to be Canadians.
There are also problems in advertising at the retail store level. How do we establish what is advertising and what is not? We know that when a retail store has a sale, it offers door openers and loss leaders. Seasonal goods are sold at reduced prices, at or below cost. Door openers are often well below cost so as to attract the crowd early in the morning, and in each department of the store a loss leader is often sold at or below cost. The other items in the department are marked up to cover the loss on the items that are sold at or below the cost price. I think it is unrealistic to try to legislate prices all across Canada, so that each item would cost the same in every part of the country. This is not the way in which our retail operation works and I do not think it should be. It would not be as interesting to go to a store if this were so.
Another matter which should be considered by the department is safety. We have covered the matter of packaging, labelling and sizes. These are difficult matters. It is difficult to establish a fair price and to legislate it. I do not think it is desirable to legislate the price of every item sold. The staff necessary to do research in this field and to follow the costs of manufacturing and the other costs involved would entail an expense outweighing the profit from the sale of the product.
I think the objectives of the department are entirely realistic in that it provides a forum for the consumer who feels that something is out of line. If the consumer feels that perhaps he is being cheated by some manufacturer, he will have someone to come to who can investigate his complaint and approach the person responsible, forcing him to reduce the price either by giving him the velvet glove treatment or by threatening adverse publicity or even, if necessary, by taking legislative action. I suggest that firm action should be the last resort.
Another problem with which the department should concern itself is that of the isolated consumer. Consumers in the more isolated parts of Canada have to pay a greater price for a product than the price for which it sells in the large centres. The fact is that the volume of sales is greater in the big city stores. The costs of transportation and freight force the price of the products up in the isolated areas. However, there is another

Corporate and Consumer Affairs question which has not been considered and which has to do with advertising. Many of the isolated consumers are out of reach of television and radio advertising. Yet the cost of advertising on radio and television as well as in the newspapers is included in the cost of the product at the manufacturing level. This part of the price is not taken off when the goods are sold in the isolated areas. I hope the new department will take into account the excess price that is being paid in these areas and will consider whether or not it is realistic. The department will also have to consider whether or not the cost of transportation is realistic. Of course this also applies to the price of eggs in Labrador, where national advertising does not reach the people.
I hope the department will also take a look at some of the adverse advertising, such as the tremendous advertising campaign which was put on to prevent consumers from buying a certain product. The department has a duty to stop such advertising, especially when it is erroneous and untrue. I am referring to a campaign which was launched recently with regard to the purchase of sealskins. The people behind the campaign are unknown to me. Perhaps it would be wrong for me to suggest that people wishing to sell another product provided the funds for this campaign. However, I do think that such advertising should be controlled by the department, as it is directed at the consumer and results in a choice of other products by the consumer.
A question which the department may find difficult to answer is the reason for the rising prices. I think the department is realistic in trying to provide a forum for the consideration of complaints of consumers. In many cases high prices are the result of inefficient management at the retail level, due to waste or loss of time. I do not think the department will be able to evaluate every single operation and say to every single inefficient manufacturer "You are inefficient and you should go out of business". Corporate and Consumer Affairs man, a family man, whose efficiency and devotion to duty have already earned him an excellent reputation.

I had the privilege to sit on that committee for several months not only in Ottawa but all across Canada as a member of the sub-committee. 1.	It is recommended further that such a joint committee be established for the life of a parliament in order to provide continuity to its work and that it should act on problems referred to it by Parliament.

3.	That increasing attention be devoted to consumer education both through the educational system and by the wider distribution of information useful to consumers through government channels.
4.	(a) That a department of consumer affairs headed by a minister be established.

Mr. Speaker, several times since Thursday, October 5, various members from Manitoba have raised in the house the question of Air Canada's announced intention to phase out the Winnipeg overhaul base. The phase out as announced would start in 1969 and conclude in 1970. On one of these occasions I posted it for an adjournment debate. I know that in speaking about this question tonight I am speaking for all members from Manitoba, for my colleagues from Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) and Springfield (Mr. Schreyer), and for my neighbours from Winnipeg South (Mr. Sherman) and Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) and, I hope, for all the other members from Manitoba-I say this trusting that the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Teil-let) is also with us on this important issue.

DEBATES	October 19, 1967
Perhaps the easiest way in which to present to the house the feelings of the people of Manitoba about this intention to close the base even earlier than was indicated would be, if there were time, to read an editorial which appeared on October 6 in the Winnipeg Free Press, a paper not noted as being opposed to the present government. There is not enough time to read it all but I should like to put two or three paragraphs on record.
When he was in Winnipeg in January 1963, Mr. George Mcllraith, then minister of transport in the Pearson government, said that the government had given a "firm guarantee" that Air Canada's overhaul base would continue to function for the next ten years. Mr. Mcllraith became quite angry at the suggestion that the base would not be kept in operation until 1973. "It's a firm fact that the base will be kept open for the next decade," he said.
His statement came two months after Prime Minister Pearson told the House of Commons that the base and its workers would remain in Manitoba until at least 1973, and then some other use might be found for it. "For at least ten years, the Winnipeg facilities will continue to be used," he promised.
I shall not take time to read the rest of the editorial. I shall not take time to recount all the statements and promises that have been made and all the rest of the things that have happened since 1948. But I do wish to express tonight the hope that the government of Canada will itself face up to this issue. Looking over the record of earlier questions I have asked about this matter I find that on February 20, 1967,1 spoke on it in an adjournment debate and pleaded with the minister who was to answer me that night, now the Registrar General (Mr. Turner), not just to send a copy of Hansard to Air Canada but to deal with this issue as a matter of government responsibility. When the hon. gentleman rose to respond to my plea, he said: "That is exactly what I am going to say tonight." The rest of his answer was to the effect that my representations would be drawn to the attention of Air Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want that tonight. None of us from Manitoba will be satisfied with that. We have had enough of it. We want the government to face up to this issue in terms of its responsibilities to the country as a whole. One of the things that has been said about the new Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer), apart from all the byplay about his being a candidate for the leadership of his party and so on, is that he wanted to get into the Department of Transport because he was interested in urban problems;
October 19, 1967

he thinks the problems of our urban communities will be particularly important in the next decade or two. We all agree. If the minister is interested in urban problems, he must be interested in those of other urban communities beside the one from which he comes-Toronto. He is bound to be interested in the affairs of Sydney, Winnipeg and the other urban areas of this country. And if he is interested in urban communities he cannot, in the first few months of his being at the head of the Department of Transport, countenance a move such as this which cannot fail to hurt the economy of Winnipeg and do a great deal of damage to relations generally, even to national unity.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not feel it is our responsibility to suggest an alternative, an answer to the problem if Air Canada cannot see its way clear to keep the overhaul base at Winnipeg. We think this should be done. We think this can be done economically at Winnipeg. We think that if Air Canada is enlarging its facilities at Dorval to take care of its new aircraft, this means it needs more space and more overhaul equipment. Why cannot this be done at Winnipeg? We believe it can.
If that is not the answer then the government, which in 1963 said "There will be no change for ten years, and if there is to be a change we will find an alternative answer to the problem," has got to deal with it. The problem has blown up in our face by this announcement that the base, instead of being phased out in 1973, is going to be phased out starting in 1969, and concluding in 1970. That is only a matter of 15 or 18 months away.
Unless the government does something to cope with the problem it is going to create a serious economic situation for Winnipeg, for Manitoba, and a very serious situation for the employees of Air Canada and their families. There is also the whole question of losing valuable technical skills we now have at Winnipeg, and this will not be good.
I see, sir, you are getting to the edge of your chair and so my seven minutes must be up, but I want to say tonight to the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport who, by the smile on his face I take it is going to answer this question, that I do not want the answer that the now Registrar General (Mr. Turner) gave last February, namely that our representations will be sent to Air Canada. We want the government to deal with this important problem because it is important not only to the workers of Air Canada, to the people of Winnipeg and to the people of Manitoba, but it is also important

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I attempted to inquire of the Minister of Transport his reasons, or the reasons of his department, for ordering the private radio station at Pond Inlet in the Northwest Territories to stop broadcasting.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
For the benefit of the parliamentary secretary and other members of the house, by way of background I might say that Pond Inlet is a small Arctic community on north Baffin
October 19, 1967

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion island. There are approximately 320 people, primarily Eskimos, who trade into this community. A radio station had been established there as a replacement for the inadequate short wave services of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's northern service. I say this, not in criticism of the C.B.C. but because the C.B.C. has been unable to establish a proper Arctic system to relay short wave in the north. The present system they have established is intended primarily to focus on South America. As I understand it, the transmitter at Sackville, which is used for the northern service, is the other end of the South American transmission system.
Certain people in this community, by their own initiative, decided they might be able to put together a small radio broadcasting station which would bring messages to people living in camps and the isolated areas. This was not a station which would meet the standards of the B.B.G. or the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It was a pirate station, if one might describe it as such, and it was not the only station of that sort in the north. However, it was technically complete. The Department of Transport, however, decided that this station should not be on the air. Possibly there was some justification for this decision, because there had been some complaints from people in certain parts of Baffin island in this respect.
The important thing at this stage is that we are dealing with the matter of communications in northern Canada. We have heard the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) in discussing her new bill, describe how it is so important to bring radio and television communication to all the people of Canada. We have heard many pious comments as to how we should extend services to the north and other isolated areas of Canada. I am not referring only to the Northwest Territories or the Yukon Territory; I am thinking of Labrador, northern Alberta, northern Saskatchewan and northern British Columbia.
When this station went on the air it was tolerated; when it became a nuisance it was told to get off the air. Despite the fact that probably the parliamentary secretary will tell me that a committee is studying this particular problem, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the Department of Transport and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development have been unable to come up with any idea which would enable them to bring adequate radio service to our people in the isolated areas of Canada.

I could tell you quite a bit about the radio station at Pond Inlet. I have here a long telegram from the people in this community describing the problems. It tells how three Eskimos who own and operate the station work eight hours a day without pay. I am not sure whether or not they are inclined to ignore the edict of the Department of Transport. I also have a telegram from the elected councillor for the eastern Arctic on the Northwest Territories Council. It is addressed to me and reads as follows:
I beg your immediate attention to the re-opening of the privately owned Pond Inlet radio station closed last week by Department of Transport due to no licence. This station has been giving a much needed service in providing communication with the outlying areas beyond the reach of C.B.C. broadcasting.
He is being rather generous in that statement, because the C.B.C. broadcast sputter and stagger on occasion.
I refer you to paragraph four of statement to council November 26 dated February 15,	1967.
Most anxious to have this station immediately granted to re-open on a temporary basis until council meets in November when the problem can be discussed and dealt with.
This telegram is signed by Simonie, a member of the Northwest Territories Council.
I could mention other isolated communities such as Baker Lake. The people of the community there decided that as a centennial project they would establish a private radio station. They started this project in 1966, making their application in the same way that people who might be interested in channel 3 in Toronto might make an application.
Of course, it was a volunteer effort and there was no cost involved. Thanks to certain elements of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, even equipment was offered to them. However, suddenly the Department of Transport, having reviewed their application wrote a four-page monologue, dialogue, document or whatever you want to call it, saying that they required further information. The letter from the department stated:
The deficiencies which have been noted in your application are as follows:
Section 1: In the event the applicant for this proposal is the "Baker Lake Resident Association", then the name of the applicant should appear opposite "(b) Incorporated company".
The letter goes on to say that the board will not recommend the issue of a licence unless the applicants therefor are Canadian
October 19, 1967
citizens. However, Mr. Speaker, this is only part of the story. The letter goes to say:
Section 9: We do not appear to have received the required technical brief in quadruplicate. This technical brief should be prepared by a broadcasting engineering consultant-
I am talking about a community of 600 people. All they want is a 20-watt radio broadcasting station so that records can be played, arrivals of aircraft announced, who is on the aircraft, community affairs, and so on. I am appealing to the minister, through his parliamentary secretary, to please consider these isolated areas of Canada. Let us do away with technicalities and red tape, so that our small communities may participate in this field in their own way.
I say to the parliamentary secretary through you, Mr. Speaker, that these people are not asking for funds from the federal or territorial treasuries. They are prepared to do this on their own, provided they can break through this little bit of red tape that seems to exist in relation to the granting of licences for radio stations and other means of communication in the north.

TRANSPORT-PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CAUSEWAY-PROVISION FOR RAILS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, usually in the adjournment debate one is only fortunate enough to have the parliamentary secretary answer his question, but tonight I feel doubly honoured in having both the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcll-raith) and his parliamentary secretary in the house. In a way this adds a feeling of assurance to the great disappointment I had this afternoon when I attempted to put what I thought was a very straightforward question to the minister in order to seek assurance from him that rail service would continue to be provided to and from the province of Prince Edward Island. I raised it in connection with a question raised yesterday afternoon by my colleague, the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) with respect to the possible inclusion or not of a railway service on the proposed causeway. Today the minister replied that since a study was still under way on the matter of the causeway he could not answer the question one way or the other. However, I asked him simply to assure the people of the province that we would continue to have rail service, whether it be by ferry or by causeway.
When I finally did get an answer, the minister said the policy of the government was well known in that regard. This is somewhat disturbing to me because I am not at all convinced that the policy is clear, and I am quite sure there is a growing amount of frustration in Prince Edward Island, both over the kind of treatment Prince Edward Islanders feel they have been receiving lately over the whole handling of the causeway

3308	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion project, and particularly over their major means of economically transporting goods and materials, namely the railway. I hope that in the next minute or so I may point out clearly to hon. members and to the minister how critical the railway service is to Prince Edward Island.
I think it is important for us to realize that we are in a unique situation with regard to the railway service. In most cases where railway traffic is used to transport goods the normal procedure is for the railway cars to be loaded, shipped from point A to point B, unloaded and reloaded again and shipped back from point B to point A. Unfortunately in Prince Edward Island we are in the rather strange dilemma of shipping as many empty freight cars off and on the island as we ship loaded ones. In normal years, for instance, we convey off the island some 28,000 railroad cars loaded with various kinds of vegetable produce and a small amount of fish, but actually we ship off the island every year some 55,000 cars, meaning that a good half of those cars are riding empty. In another time of the year we bring to the island bulk fuels, fertilizers, construction materials and things of that nature, but unfortunately there is no freight to send back. Therefore, if the possibility of abandoning rail traffic was even remotely contemplated by those who are designing the transportation system of the future, as it will affect Prince Edward Island, this would mean that we would have to carry by truck all our major materials, both the goods that we ship to market and goods we must import. This would mean that we would have to ask a major trucking firm to transport empty vehicles half the time. I know of no trucking firm in this country or any other that could do that and offer an economic service to the user.
I have been told by people who are in the business of analysing these matters that even were we to provide 65 per cent back freight, our shipping costs would immediately double and, in many cases, triple. Those who are familiar with the difficulties we encounter in the maritimes know that we have great problems associated with transportation rates that are levied against our goods. Even though we have received special consideration in the past, some of which unfortunately has disappeared in the last few months, we have just barely maintained a competitive position. One shudders to think, Mr. Speaker, what would occur in Prince Edward Island and to its economy if we were suddenly to be faced

DEBATES	October 19, 19G7
with double or triple transportation costs on our major products.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer also to what I regard as a major moral and economic commitment to the province as laid out in the terms of confederation, a contract or a covenant between the province of Prince Edward Island and the government of Canada. There was a covenant to provide continuous communication with the mainland; and by "communication" I do not mean a phone call, a telegram or a letter. I mean the transporting of individuals and goods to and from that province.
If there is to be even the slightest cessation or the slightest retardation of our service to Prince Edward Island, in my opinion, it will be a major default, in the federal government's responsibility to our tiniest province. Frankly, I have been disturbed by the attitude which has seemed to exist on the part of Canadian National Railways in terms of the way in which they have looked after their roadbed on the island over the past few years, and the number of substations that have been phased out. I realize that in dealing with these specific issues I should turn my attention to another minister. However, I am hoping to hear from the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith) a very strong assurance regarding future designs, either by ferry service or causeway, which will assure the island of railway service as long as it is economically and socially necessary.
